## Discussion

### Prior sensitivity and the limits of "the data will overwhelm the prior"

A common expectation in applied Bayesian work is that, with enough data, the posterior converges to what the likelihood alone would say regardless of the prior. That expectation is asymptotic: it holds as sample size grows large relative to the number of parameters being estimated, provided the prior does not rule out the data-favored value outright. Neither condition is automatically met in a design of this kind, and the salinity effect on attack rate in this reanalysis is a concrete illustration of why.

Four features of the present model work against the asymptotic expectation, none of them unusual for a controlled ecological experiment. First, the sample bearing on any one contrast is smaller than the nominal sample size suggests: 56 cell means inform roughly 33 free parameters jointly, and a specific pairwise contrast such as "20 g/L vs. 30 g/L" draws on only the subset of that data connected to those two levels. Second, the elicited priors are not vague. They were built from stated, literature-anchored fold-change claims (@sec-priors) specifically so that they would carry real information; a prior built to be informative should not be expected to vanish in the face of a likelihood that is itself only moderately informative at this sample size. Third, and specific to this model's structure, the zero-sum parameterization used for every main effect and interaction (@sec-stat-mdl) couples the levels of a factor rather than estimating them independently: a shift favored at one level must be compensated elsewhere in the same factor for the sum-to-zero constraint to hold, so tension between prior and likelihood at one level can surface as tension in the opposite direction at another, as it did here between 20 and 30 g/L. None of these conditions is exotic. They are close to the default case for a small controlled experiment estimating a richly structured effect, which is precisely the setting this paper's proposed workflow is meant for.

The practical resolution in this case came from checking directly rather than assuming an answer in either direction. Power-scaling sensitivity (`psense`) on the salinity effect on attack rate flagged genuine prior-data conflict, not mere weak identification, at both 20 and 30 g/L. Read alone, that flag could support two opposite misreadings: that the reported salinity effect is a prior artifact and should be discounted, or — because the flag arrived after an earlier, differently-configured fit had produced the opposite sign — that no conclusion about salinity's direction is possible at all. Neither followed once the salinity prior's width was swept across a range spanning tighter than elicited to the original, non-differentiated pre-elicitation value: the sign of the 20–30 attack-rate contrast held throughout that range, and its magnitude grew rather than shrank as the prior's pull was loosened, indicating the elicited prior is if anything conservative relative to what the likelihood alone favors. The coefficient-level conflict `psense` detected is real and is reported as such, but it does not extend to the derived, interpretable quantity the paper actually reports a conclusion about.

The general lesson is not that priors are dangerous or that Bayesian estimation is fragile; it is that "the data will sort it out" is an assumption, not a property that can be taken for granted in a small, multi-parameter design, and that the check is inexpensive relative to the alternative of either an unexamined false confidence or an unexamined false alarm. This is offered as a second, narrower illustration alongside the paper's central one: just as @nandini2026's own analysis benefited from an inferential layer that reports uncertainty rather than a threshold decision, the model built here benefits from treating its own prior choices as a further hypothesis to be checked against the data, rather than as a settled input. The reconciliation was extended to both pairwise salinity contrasts on attack rate (20 g/L vs. 30 g/L and 10 g/L vs. 30 g/L), which tracked one another closely across the swept range — a coherence check consistent with 10 and 20 g/L being themselves indistinguishable.

The prey$\times$salinity interaction cells that the same power-scaling check flagged received the equivalent sweep as well, on a derived quantity asking whether the 20–30 g/L attack-rate gap differs by prey (Nitokra vs. Apocyclops; Brachionus vs. Apocyclops; reported on the primary fit in @sec-attack-rate), and the outcome there differed in kind rather than degree. The Nitokra-vs-Apocyclops contrast is a stable non-finding: its HDI includes zero at every swept interaction-prior width, from tighter than elicited through markedly looser. The Brachionus-vs-Apocyclops contrast is directionally consistent — negative throughout — but its HDI excludes zero only at the loosest width tested (0.70), well past the elicited value (0.35), and includes zero at that elicited value itself. This is the reverse of the salinity main effect's pattern: there, widening the prior strengthened an interval that already excluded zero; here, widening the prior is what produces exclusion in the first place, so the apparent finding depends on adopting a prior looser than the one actually built from background knowledge, not on a robustness margin around it. Accordingly, this paper does not report a confirmed prey-dependent salinity effect on attack rate. The interaction term is retained in the model because the causal graph motivates it structurally (@sec-stat-mdl), but its magnitude is not treated as an established result. The asymmetry between the two checks — the salinity main effect surviving, the interaction not — is itself the clearest illustration in this reanalysis that a sensitivity check is not a formality to be passed on the way to a predetermined conclusion: it returns whichever answer is actually there, and reporting follows that answer rather than the other way around.
